To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
fathers in wild baboon societies buffer offspring from the negative effects of the social and ecological environments, and facilitate offspring access to food.

(1) juvenile baboons actively manage associations with their genetic father, (2) father offspring associations increase when other males are in sight, (3), father offspring associations are strongest among subordinate males, and (4), father offspring associations facilitate juvenile access to richer food patches.

(1) father offspring associations in a promiscuously breeding mammal are mediated by offspring active choices that are sensitive to the presence of other adult males and the mother’s absence, (2) such father offspring associations facilitate access to food for offspring, and (3) father- offspring associations are stronger when fathers are subordinate.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the evolution of paternal care and its effects on offspring fitness in a promiscuously breeding primate species.
the evolution of paternal care and how fathers may buffer the environment faced by their young in wild baboon societies.
understanding the evolution and function of paternal care.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the presence of the father in promiscuous societies can have a significant positive effect on the survival of their offspring.
the father-offspring associations are a result of the father being more tolerant of his offspring, which in turn enables the offspring to access richer food sources.
the presence of a father may improve the access of offspring to resources in a wild promiscuous primated society.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
paternal effects are mediated by the ability of fathers to provide access to resources for their offspring.
fathers may buffer their offspring against risks of attacks by conspecifics and predators, and improve their access to food in a wild primate society.

paternal care can evolve even in promiscuous societies if the father can provide benefits that are not accessible to other males, and that these benefits can be provided in the form of protection from predators and other threats, or access to resources.
The main takeaway from our work is that
fathers may buffer their offspring from the negative effects of the social and ecological environments.
paternal effects are not restricted to biparentally caring species, but may also be important in species with low paternal investment.
paternal care can evolve in species where paternity confidence is low.
